title: Blog 1 - AWS CLI and AWS MCP Server in the Vibe Coding Era
content:
AWS CLI in the Vibe Coding Era: From Manual Commands to AWS MCP Server Engineers traditionally interact with AWS by typing individual aws commands in a terminal. In the Vibe Coding era, developers increasingly ask coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, or Kiro to build systems from natural-language instructions. This changes how command-line access to AWS should be designed and governed.
1. Why AWS CLI still matters The AWS Command Line Interface is an open-source tool for managing AWS services from Linux/macOS shells, Windows CMD or PowerShell, and remote environments such as EC2 or Systems Manager.
It remains essential because it:
Provides command-line access to most capabilities available in the AWS Management Console. Calls public AWS APIs directly for fast, precise resource inspection. Fits naturally into scripts and CI/CD pipelines for repeatable automation. 2. Three risks when agents generate AWS CLI commands Stale knowledge An LLM may not know recently released services, properties, or flags and can invent syntax when working from training data alone.
Using CLI instead of Infrastructure as Code Agents often generate a sequence of imperative commands for infrastructure. This may work for a demo, but it is harder to review, reproduce, roll back, and manage than AWS CDK or AWS CloudFormation.
Overly broad IAM permissions Generated scripts may request excessive access simply to make a task succeed. That convenience creates a serious production risk.
3. AWS MCP Server and Agent Toolkit for AWS AWS MCP Server is an AWS-managed remote MCP server that gives coding agents focused tools instead of requiring them to recall commands:
search_documentation and read_documentation retrieve current AWS guidance. call_aws invokes AWS API operations with the caller’s IAM credentials. run_script executes short Python code in a server-side sandbox to combine and filter API calls in one round trip; the sandbox has no network, local filesystem, or shell access. Skills encode service-specific practices maintained by AWS teams. 4. Safety controls Authenticate requests with IAM SigV4 through mcp-proxy-for-aws. Separate human and agent permissions with IAM policies or SCPs; agents can be restricted to read-only access. Monitor MCP metrics in Amazon CloudWatch and audit API calls through AWS CloudTrail. AWS MCP Server has no separate service charge; normal resource and data-transfer charges still apply. Takeaway AWS CLI remains valuable for quick operations and automation. Core infrastructure should be managed as code, while agents should access AWS through AWS MCP Server with explicit IAM guardrails instead of executing guessed commands.
References What is the AWS Command Line Interface? — AWS Documentation The AWS MCP Server is now generally available — AWS News Blog Image source — AWS News Blog

title: Blog 2 - Infrastructure as Code and AWS IaC MCP Server
content:
Vibe Coding AWS Infrastructure: Why Infrastructure as Code and AWS IaC MCP Server Matter AI can produce application code quickly. Letting an agent provision AWS infrastructure through disconnected commands, however, often creates systems that work in a demo but are difficult to control in production. Vibe Coders therefore need a solid Infrastructure as Code foundation.
1. Infrastructure as Code on AWS Infrastructure as Code defines AWS resources in versioned files so deployments are consistent, repeatable, and easier to govern.
AWS provides two widely used native options:
AWS CloudFormation declares infrastructure in JSON or YAML templates. AWS Cloud Development Kit lets developers define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, and other familiar languages before synthesizing CloudFormation. Asking an agent to produce CloudFormation or AWS CDK makes changes reviewable in Git and provides a clearer lifecycle than a sequence of AWS CLI commands.
2. Three common bottlenecks Stale or incorrect resource properties Without live documentation, an agent may use invalid properties or miss current best practices.
Excessive tool switching Engineers move repeatedly among documentation, linters, deployment consoles, and logs during each authoring and validation cycle.
Slow deployment troubleshooting A stack may end in AccessDenied or ROLLBACK_COMPLETE without clearly identifying the missing permission, forcing engineers to correlate CloudFormation events with AWS CloudTrail.
3. AWS Infrastructure as Code MCP Server AWS IaC MCP Server runs locally over stdio and supports MCP-compatible assistants through a four-stage workflow:
Author Documentation, sample, and construct search tools help agents use current CloudFormation/CDK schemas and recommended patterns.
Validate validate_cloudformation_template wraps cfn-lint for structure and schema checks. check_cloudformation_template_compliance wraps cfn-guard for controls such as S3 encryption, Block Public Access, and log retention. These checks run locally without AWS permissions.
Deploy Validated templates are deployed with AWS CLI. Pre-deployment validation can be configured before creating a change set.
Troubleshoot troubleshoot_cloudformation_deployment correlates stack events with CloudTrail to identify missing permissions such as iam:PassRole.
4. Operational guidance Validation requires no AWS permissions; troubleshooting needs only read access to CloudFormation and CloudTrail. Troubleshooting data sent to an AI model provider must follow organizational data-handling rules. CloudTrail events may take 5–15 minutes to appear after a failed deployment. Takeaway Production-oriented Vibe Coding on AWS should use CloudFormation or AWS CDK, with AWS IaC MCP Server closing the Author → Validate → Deploy → Troubleshoot loop.
References Accelerate CloudFormation development with the IaC MCP Server — AWS DevOps Blog Introducing the AWS Infrastructure as Code MCP Server — AWS DevOps Blog Image source — AWS DevOps Blog

The Enterprise Knowledge Challenge: Identifying the challenges of fragmented enterprise knowledge—scattered documents across silos, inconsistent search accuracy, and knowledge decay as teams scale. Building an Enterprise Knowledge Hub: Architecting a centralized knowledge hub on AWS Cloud, standardizing ingestion, indexing, and synchronization pipelines for AI-powered consumption. Retrieval and Intelligence: Combining Retrieval (RAG) techniques with foundation models to deliver context-aware answers, reduce hallucinations, and accelerate internal knowledge discovery. Security and Governance: Applying enterprise security and data governance controls—enforcing role-based access control, protecting sensitive information, and maintaining compliance boundaries. Delivery and Proven Results: Measuring real-world impact after rollout, including search efficiency, response accuracy, and operational productivity gains. Roadmap to Enterprise Adoption: Structuring a practical roadmap from initial proof-of-concept (PoC) to full-scale enterprise adoption across teams. Event Photo Key Takeaways & Personal Contribution Data Architecture Drives AI Quality: For enterprise AI applications, organizing a reliable Enterprise Knowledge Hub and Retrieval pipeline is just as critical as model selection. Security & Governance by Design: Integrating internal documents into RAG workflows requires strict access control so users only retrieve information they are authorized to view. Phased Production Roadmap: Moving from PoC to enterprise adoption with measurable metrics provides a practical blueprint applicable to designing scalable AI pipelines in my OJT internship.

title: Blog 3 - Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Harness
content:
What Is an AWS Agent Harness? Taking AI Agents from Demo to Production with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Building an AI agent that runs on a laptop is no longer especially difficult. Production introduces the real challenge: the model needs a sandbox, memory, tools and MCP connections, identity, concurrency controls, logs, traces, and deterministic checks around risky actions. The orchestration layer around the model is the Agent Harness.
1. What is an Agent Harness? An AI agent is typically an LLM calling tools in a loop to achieve a goal. Production complexity comes from connecting that loop safely to:
Sandboxed command and code execution. Cross-session memory. Tools, skills, and MCP servers. Identity and authorization. Concurrency and session storage. Logs, traces, evaluations, and risk controls. An Agent Harness is the orchestration and operational layer that turns those separate pieces into a configurable, scalable platform.
2. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Harness Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Harness packages production capabilities behind CreateHarness and InvokeHarness.
Models The harness supports models on Amazon Bedrock and external providers. A session can switch models without losing context, while external provider keys are stored in the AgentCore Identity token vault.
Tools and Skills Configuration can attach AgentCore Gateway, remote MCP servers, AgentCore Browser, Code Interpreter, and inline functions for human-in-the-loop steps. Skills can be loaded from AWS Skills, Git repositories, Amazon S3, or containers.
Memory and isolated runtime Managed memory supports semantic retrieval and summarization while separating users by actorId. Sessions run in isolated Firecracker microVMs and can use managed session storage, Amazon EFS, or Amazon S3 Files.
Observability, evaluation, and export Logs and traces feed CloudWatch GenAI Observability. AgentCore Evaluations measures quality, endpoint versions support staging, production, and rollback, and advanced users can export a harness into Strands code.
3. Strands defaults and Lifecycle Hooks Recent capabilities include:
Prompt caching, conversation summarization, and context offloading to reduce token usage. Built-in tools such as todo_write, subagent, and web_fetch, with separate read, write, and edit permissions. Four lifecycle hooks: before_invocation, before_tool_call, after_tool_call, and after_invocation. Lifecycle hooks add deterministic policy checks. A Lambda function attached to before_tool_call can reject refunds above a threshold, with failureMode defaulting to deny when the check fails or times out. Hooks can also publish asynchronous events to Amazon SNS or Amazon EventBridge.
4. Cost and permission controls Harness itself has no separate charge; users pay for underlying components and consumed resources. AgentCore Runtime charges for active CPU and memory consumption, with pricing varying by Region. Leaving allowedTools empty or setting a wildcard can make future built-in tools available automatically. Applications with fixed boundaries should list explicit tools and protect high-risk actions with before_tool_call hooks. Takeaway The difference between an agent demo and a production agent lies in the harness. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Harness combines isolated runtime, managed memory, tools, observability, evaluation, and lifecycle hooks so teams can control reliability, security, and cost without rebuilding the entire orchestration layer.
References Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness is now generally available — AWS AI Blog AgentCore harness adds Strands defaults, built-in tools, and lifecycle hooks — AWS AI Blog Image source — AWS AI Blog

title: Sharing and Feedback
content:
Joining the First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) program has been an important stepping stone in bridging academic study at FPT University with practical AWS engineering standards. Beyond helping me systematically build foundational Cloud knowledge, the program kept me up to date with emerging trends in Generative AI, RAG, and Agentic AI through its curriculum, community, and live events.
Overall Evaluation 1. Overall Satisfaction: Very Satisfied (5/5).
What I valued most was being able to connect the lessons to the team project. The labs helped me get familiar with individual services. In the SEAL project, I had to think about how those services fit together and how to verify that the processing flow worked. Keeping a weekly worklog helped me see what I had practiced and where I needed more time.
2. Learning Progression
A well-structured learning progression from Cloud fundamentals (Cloud Foundations, VPC, EC2, S3, IAM) to modern services (Serverless, Event-Driven, AI/GenAI).
The early lessons showed me how networking, permissions, and storage fit into an AWS system. When I reached Lambda and SQS, that foundation helped me understand why SEAL used a queue between receiving submissions and grading them with AI. I also had the chance to deploy a model with Ollama and Qwen3 on EC2 and measure its processing time.
3. Security and Cost Governance
Strong emphasis on security and cost governance from the very first labs (MFA, IAM Least Privilege, AWS Budgets, and resource clean-up).
The labs made checking IAM permissions, setting budget alerts, and cleaning up resources part of my routine. In the AI grading project, the same mindset led to questions about which data the worker should access and how to keep sensitive information out of model inputs. Working on the data preparation step showed me how those decisions shape the processing flow.
4. Community and Events
The AWS Study Group VN community and in-person events (Buildathon Kick-off, AWS Cloud & AI Day Hanoi, Community Day) create an open, supportive environment to learn directly from mentors and practitioners.
Writing three technical posts helped me learn in a different way. To explain AWS MCP Server, IaC, and AgentCore Harness to readers who were new to the topics, I had to revisit the documentation and think carefully about how to describe what each tool does. I want to keep improving that skill alongside my confidence in live presentations.
Additional Questions Would I Recommend FCAJ to Friends? Why?
Definitely YES.
Why: FCAJ provides a proactive, industry-aligned learning environment that stays closely connected to fast-moving technologies—especially Cloud + AI. Beyond preparing for AWS certifications, the program builds strong habits in technical writing, community sharing, and architectural thinking, which are invaluable for any IT/AI student entering the industry.
For someone new to cloud, I would suggest following the lessons in order, repeating the main lab steps, and writing down one thing they learned each time. For someone interested in AI, the team project is a chance to put a model into a workflow that uses storage, a queue, and monitoring.
Suggestions & Expectations The volume of labs and lessons becomes fairly dense during the middle weeks; adding concise cheat-sheets of common IAM and VPC misconfigurations per module would help newcomers troubleshoot faster. Extending the duration of short Hands-on mini challenges during offline events would give attendees more time for direct, on-the-spot Q&A with mentors. I would also like a group lab that runs through an entire workflow, from submitting data and queuing a job to running an AI grader and checking the result and logs. At the end, each group could share one design decision and one issue they ran into, then compare how they handled them.
